title: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
summary: How ACORN keeps HNSW search fast under arbitrary filters: predicate subgraph traversal, gamma-expanded neighbor lists, M_beta compression with two-hop recovery, ACORN-1, and the pre-filter fallback.
outcomes: Explain why strict filtered search on a normal HNSW graph gets stuck and why HNSW pruning is unsafe for predicates
Compute expected passing neighbors per node and the chance a node becomes a dead end at a given selectivity
Trace ACORN-gamma's compression rule and the two-hop lookup that recovers pruned neighbors
Compare ACORN-gamma and ACORN-1 on build time, memory and search speed using the paper's numbers
Choose gamma from a minimum selectivity and decide when a query should fall back to pre-filtering

lessons.title: Why a filter breaks greedy search on an HNSW graph

blocks.md: A **hybrid query** asks for the $K$ nearest vectors that also satisfy a structured predicate, such as `category = shoes AND price < 50`. The **selectivity** $s$ of the predicate is the fraction of records that pass it. The ACORN paper (Patel, Kraft, Guestrin, Zaharia, SIGMOD 2024) names three ways to answer such queries and argues all three fall short.

From the previous course: **pre-filtering** finds every passing record and brute-forces them, costing $O(sn)$ distance computations, which is exact but linear in $sn$. **Post-filtering** searches the unfiltered HNSW index and drops failing results, so it must over-fetch about $K/s$ candidates, and it degrades badly when passing vectors sit far from the query. **Specialized indices** such as Filtered-DiskANN and NHQ build the filter into the graph, but only for small sets of equality filters known in advance.

Besides selectivity and dataset size, the paper studies a third workload property that hurts post-filtering: **query correlation**. If the passing points cluster near the query (positive correlation), post-filtering finds them quickly. If they cluster far away (negative correlation), the unfiltered search walks toward the wrong region, and the paper notes the worst case is $O(n)$.

Now the obvious fix: during graph search, just ignore neighbors that fail the predicate and only walk among passing nodes. This is **predicate subgraph traversal**: searching the subgraph induced by the passing points $X_p$. It only computes distances for passing nodes, so it never wastes work on failures. The figure shows what happens when you try it on an ordinary graph.

blocks.title: Strict filtered search on a plain graph gets stuck

scenes.caption: Ten points on a grid, each linked to its 2 nearest points (M = 2, ties broken alphabetically). Green nodes pass the filter (5 of 10, so s = 0.5). Badges are distances to the query for passing nodes. The true filtered answer is B at 3.16.
Search starts at the entry point I (7.81). Strict filtering means we only step onto, and only compute distances for, nodes that pass. I has one passing neighbor: H.
At H (5.83) the neighbors are A, G and I. A and G fail the filter, and I is farther than H. Greedy search stops and returns H, missing B, D and J entirely.
Why: this is the predicate subgraph, only passing nodes and edges between them. It splits into three pieces, {I, H}, {D, B} and {J} alone. J has zero passing neighbors.

The real route to B runs H, G, J, E, D, B. G and E fail the filter, so strict traversal cannot use them. The overall nearest point, E (2.24), also fails, which is why post-filtering would waste work here.

blocks.prompt: In the plain graph ($M = 2$) each node has 2 or 3 links and $s = 0.5$. Suppose a node's neighbors pass independently with probability $s$. What is the chance that a node with exactly 2 neighbors has no passing neighbor at all?
blocks.reveal: $(1-s)^2 = 0.5^2 = 0.25$. One node in four is a dead end, which is exactly what happened to J. With degree $d$ the chance is $(1-s)^d$, so the fix is to make $d$ large enough that $(1-s)^d$ is tiny. That is the core of ACORN-$\gamma$.

blocks.md: HNSW's construction makes this worse. Its neighbor heuristic prunes the edge $v$ to $b$ whenever some kept neighbor $a$ is closer to $b$ than $v$ is, expecting search to reach $b$ through $a$. That pruning is **metadata-blind**: if $v$ and $b$ pass the predicate but $a$ fails, the detour no longer exists in the predicate subgraph, and the edge was pruned for nothing.

The paper frames the goal with an **oracle partition index**: if you knew the predicate at build time, you would build a separate HNSW over just $X_p$ and search it in about $O(\log(sn) + K)$. That beats both pre- and post-filtering at every selectivity and correlation, but one index per possible predicate is impossible when predicates are regexes, date ranges, or keyword lists. ACORN's aim is to make *any* predicate subgraph of one shared index behave like that oracle HNSW.

Predicate subgraph traversal is the right search strategy (no distance computations wasted on failing nodes), but on a normal HNSW graph the predicate subgraph is sparse and disconnected. ACORN changes how the graph is built, or how neighbors are looked up, so that the predicate subgraph stays connected for any predicate.

blocks.question: In the figure, strict filtered search returns H. Which change to the search alone (same graph) would reliably find B?
options: Increase ef so the candidate list holds more passing nodes
Start from a different fixed entry point chosen at build time
Step through failing nodes such as G and E with a beam of ef 2 or more, at the cost of computing their distances
Truncate each neighbor list to M before filtering
blocks.explain: From I the only reachable passing nodes are I and H, so a bigger ef cannot help: there is nothing else in the predicate subgraph component to add. Walking through failing nodes reaches B but spends distance computations on non-results, which is the in-traversal filtering cost ACORN wants to avoid. A fixed entry point does not know the predicate.

blocks.question: A workload filters images by label 'cat' while queries are photos of dogs, so passing points sit far from each query. Which baseline suffers most?
options: Pre-filtering, because selectivity drops
Post-filtering, because the unfiltered search heads toward the wrong region
Neither, since both are exact
The oracle partition index
blocks.explain: This is negative query correlation. Post-filtering's unfiltered search converges near dog photos that fail the filter, and it must expand very far to collect K cats. Pre-filtering's cost depends only on how many records pass, not on where they sit.

lessons.title: ACORN-gamma: expand every neighbor list by gamma

blocks.md: ACORN-$\gamma$ makes two changes to HNSW construction. First, **neighbor list expansion**: where HNSW collects $M$ candidate edges per node, ACORN-$\gamma$ collects $M \cdot \gamma$ approximate nearest neighbors, found with an ordinary (metadata-agnostic) search over the graph built so far. Second, it **drops HNSW's RNG-style pruning** on those lists, because that pruning is metadata-blind. So each level approximates a kNN graph rather than a relative neighborhood graph.

The search changes in one place: the neighbor lookup. At each visited node $v$ on level $l$, ACORN scans $N^l(v)$, keeps only neighbors that pass the predicate, giving the filtered list $N^l_p(v)$, and **truncates it to the first $M$**. Everything else is HNSW's greedy beam search with candidate list size ef. The truncation keeps the per-node cost bounded by $M$ distance computations, just as in HNSW, even though the stored list is $\gamma$ times longer.
Why $\gamma$? If a node's $M\gamma$ neighbors pass independently with probability $s$ (no predicate clustering, which the paper treats as the worst case), the number that pass is binomial with mean:

blocks.tex: \mathbb{E}\,|N^l_p(v)| = |N^l(v)| \cdot s = \gamma M s \;\geq\; M \quad\text{whenever}\quad s \geq s_{\min} = \frac{1}{\gamma}
blocks.caption: Choose gamma = 1/s_min, the lowest selectivity you plan to serve with the graph. Then every predicate at or above s_min yields a predicate subgraph whose expected degree is at least M.

blocks.title: Expected passing neighbors per node vs selectivity

curves.label: ACORN list (gamma x M x s)

scenes.caption: M = 32, gamma = 12 (the paper's SIFT1M setting). At s = 1/12 an ACORN list of 384 expects 32 passing neighbors, exactly M, while HNSW's 64-slot bottom list expects only 5.33.
gamma = 30 (the LAION setting) moves s_min down to 1/30 = 0.033. Below s_min even the expanded list expects fewer than M passing neighbors, which is where ACORN hands the query to pre-filtering.
gamma = 1 is plain HNSW density: the green line drops onto M x s and the predicate subgraph only has degree M when nearly everything passes.

blocks.md: The expected value is not the whole story: the chance that a node gets **zero** passing neighbors, and so becomes a dead end like J, is $(1-s)^{M\gamma}$. With $M = 32$ and $s = 1/12$, HNSW's upper-level list of $M = 32$ has a 6.2% chance of being empty and its bottom list of 64 a 0.38% chance. ACORN-$\gamma$ with $\gamma = 12$ has 384 slots: $(11/12)^{384} \approx 3.1 \times 10^{-15}$. The paper bounds the probability that any node on the search path disconnects by $O(\log n \cdot (1-s)^{M\gamma})$, which decays exponentially in $\gamma$.

blocks.title: ACORN-gamma: denser lists keep the subgraph connected

scenes.caption: Same points, now built with gamma = 2: each node keeps its M x gamma = 4 nearest points instead of 2 (21 edges instead of 12). Simplified: one layer, kNN links, no HNSW levels.
The predicate subgraph now has edges H to J and J to D, so the five passing nodes form one chain: I, H, J, D, B. Expected passing neighbors per node: M x gamma x s = 4 x 0.5 = 2 = M.
Search from I (7.81). Its list is A, C, G, H. Filter it to passing nodes, keep at most M = 2: only H. Move to H (5.83). No distance is computed for A, C or G.
At H the list is A, G, I, J. Passing: I and J. J (4.12) is closer than H, so move to J.
At J the list is D, E, G, H. Passing: D and H. D (3.61) is closer, move to D.
At D the passing neighbors are B and J. B (3.16) is closer. At B the only passing neighbor is D (3.61), farther, so search stops and returns B, the true filtered nearest neighbor.

blocks.md: **Getting into the subgraph.** ACORN keeps HNSW's single fixed entry point, which may fail the predicate. Search runs in two stages. In stage 1 it filters each upper level's neighbor list and drops a level whenever the filtered list is empty. Because the expansion makes upper levels dense, any level with fewer than $M\gamma$ nodes is fully connected, so as soon as a level holds one passing node, the search reaches it in one hop. Stage 2 is then greedy search over the predicate subgraph.

The paper's analysis gives an expected search cost of $O((d+\gamma)\log(sn) + \log(1/s))$ for vector dimension $d$, close to the oracle partition's $O(d \log(sn))$. The $\gamma$ term is the cheap predicate check over up to $M\gamma$ stored neighbors per visited node; distances are still computed for at most $M$.

Misconception: "just raise M in HNSW". The paper notes that Qdrant's earlier densification idea did this, but $M$ also sets HNSW's level multiplier $m_L = 1/\ln M$, so raising it flattens the hierarchy, and HNSW is sensitive to its number of levels. ACORN keeps $M$ (and therefore $m_L$ and the level structure) fixed and expands the lists by $\gamma$ instead.

blocks.question: An index is built with M = 32 and gamma = 12. A query arrives with predicate selectivity s = 0.25. Roughly how many neighbors will the search compute distances for at a typical visited node?
options: 384, the whole stored list
96, all passing neighbors
At most 32: the passing neighbors are truncated to M
blocks.explain: About 384 x 0.25 = 96 neighbors pass, but ACORN truncates the filtered list to the first M = 32 before computing distances. The predicate is evaluated on up to 384 entries (cheap), distances on at most 32 (expensive). 8 would be plain HNSW's expectation.

blocks.question: Why does ACORN-gamma skip HNSW's RNG-based pruning when building neighbor lists?
options: It makes construction too slow
The pruned detour through a third node may fail the predicate, so the shortcut it relied on vanishes in the predicate subgraph
RNG pruning only works for cosine distance
HNSW never prunes at the bottom level
blocks.explain: HNSW drops edge v to b if some kept neighbor a is closer to b, trusting search to go v, a, b. For a predicate where v and b pass but a fails, that path does not exist. Without knowing predicates at build time you cannot prune safely, so ACORN keeps the near neighbors and uses a predicate-agnostic compression instead.

lessons.title: Paying for density: M_beta compression and two-hop recovery

blocks.md: Expanding every list by $\gamma$ costs memory and build time. HNSW-style indexes live in RAM, so a $\gamma = 12$ index that stored 384 neighbors per node on the bottom level would be several times larger than HNSW. ACORN-$\gamma$ attacks this where it matters most: the **bottom level**, which holds every node. Upper levels are small because a node reaches level $l$ with probability $M^{-l}$.

The idea is to store each node's nearby neighbors exactly and approximate the farther ones through two-hop lookups. A tunable parameter $M_\beta$ (between 0 and $M\gamma$) sets how many of the closest candidates are kept unconditionally. For the remaining candidates, in distance order, ACORN keeps a set $H$ of the chosen nodes' neighbors and applies one rule:

1. If candidate $c$ is already in $H$, prune it (some kept neighbor already links to it).
2. Otherwise keep $c$ and add all of $c$'s neighbors to $H$.
3. Stop when the candidates run out or when $|H|$ plus the number of chosen edges exceeds $M\gamma$.

$H$ is thrown away after construction. Nothing in this rule looks at metadata, so it is **predicate-agnostic**.

scenes.caption: Node v's candidate edges, nearest first. M = 3, gamma = 2, so there are M x gamma = 6 candidates. M_beta = 2. Known neighbor lists: c links to d, x, y; e links to f, z.
The first M_beta = 2 candidates, a and b, are kept unconditionally. These are the closest neighbors and are stored exactly.
c is not in H, so keep it and add its neighbors d, x, y to H. Chosen edges + |H| = 3 + 3 = 6, which does not exceed M x gamma = 6, so continue.
d is already in H (it is a neighbor of kept node c), so the edge v to d is pruned. Search can still find d two hops away, through c.
e is not in H: keep it and add f, z. Now 4 chosen + |H| = 5 gives 9 > 6, so pruning stops. f is never stored, but it is in H, reachable through e.
Stored list: a, b, c, e (4 slots, not 6). At search time, entries past position M_beta (c and e) are expanded to their own lists, so for a predicate passing b, d and f the lookup recovers b, d, f.

blocks.md: **Search-time recovery.** The compression-aware lookup at node $v$ has two phases. For the first $M_\beta$ entries of $N^l(v)$ it just filters, as before. For entries past position $M_\beta$, it also expands each one into its own neighbor list (neighbors of neighbors) and filters those. The pruning rule guarantees that any node $x$ pruned from $v$'s list sits in the list of some neighbor $y$ of $v$ at a position beyond $M_\beta$, so the expansion finds $x$ whatever the predicate is.

blocks.title: Neighbor storage per node, SIFT1M settings

scenes.caption: Bottom-level slots per node. HNSW stores 2M = 64. ACORN-gamma with gamma = 12 would store M x gamma = 384. With compression the paper measures an average of 87.5 on SIFT1M (Table 6).

Bytes per node with 4-byte ids, counting average edges. Upper levels add 32/31 = 1.03 slots (HNSW) and 384/31 = 12.4 (ACORN). Totals: 260, 1586, 400. The reference code reserves M_beta + 1.5M = 112 level-0 slots, so real size is larger.

blocks.md: In the paper's measurements this keeps the overhead modest. Table 5 reports ACORN-$\gamma$ index sizes at most about 1.3x HNSW (SIFT1M: 0.98 GB vs 0.75 GB including vectors). Build time is the bigger cost: the paper's construction complexity is $O(n\gamma\log n\log\gamma)$ versus HNSW's $O(n \log n)$, and Table 4 shows SIFT1M taking 148.9 s vs 11.3 s for HNSW. Figure 12 shows search quality is fairly insensitive to $M_\beta$, so the paper uses $M_\beta = M$ or $2M$, while plain HNSW pruning on the same lists badly hurts hybrid search.

Upper levels stay uncompressed with up to $M\gamma$ neighbors (the paper's Table 6 shows level 1 at exactly 384 = $M\gamma$ on SIFT1M). That density is what makes small upper levels fully connected, which is how stage 1 of search finds a passing node quickly.

blocks.prompt: With M = 32, what fraction of nodes appear on level 1 or higher in an HNSW-style level assignment, and so would pay for an uncompressed 384-slot upper list?
blocks.reveal: A node's top level is $\lfloor -\ln(u)\, m_L \rfloor$ with $m_L = 1/\ln M$, so $P(\text{level} \geq 1) = e^{-1/m_L} = 1/M = 1/32 \approx 3.1\%$. Expected upper-level slots per node are $M\gamma \sum_{l \geq 1} M^{-l} = 384/31 \approx 12.4$. That is why compressing only level 0 captures most of the savings.

blocks.question: During compression, candidate d is pruned from v's list because it is in H. At search time, under a predicate where d passes but kept neighbor c (which links to d) fails, can the search still reach d from v?
options: No, because c fails the predicate and is skipped
Yes, if c sits beyond position M_beta, because the lookup expands c's list before filtering
Only if d is within the first M_beta entries
Only with ACORN-1
blocks.explain: The two-hop expansion reads c's neighbor list regardless of whether c passes; the predicate is applied to the expanded entries. By construction, any pruned node was in H only because some later kept neighbor links to it, and entries past M_beta are exactly the ones the lookup expands.

blocks.question: You double M_beta from 32 to 64 on LAION. What is the main effect?
options: Bottom-level lists get longer and the index larger, with little change in search quality according to the paper
The minimum supported selectivity halves
Upper levels become compressed
Search switches from ACORN-gamma to ACORN-1
blocks.explain: M_beta is the number of nearest candidates stored without pruning on the compressed level, so raising it grows the bottom-level lists. The paper finds search fairly insensitive to M_beta (Figure 12). s_min is set by gamma, not M_beta.

lessons.title: ACORN-1: expand at search time instead of build time

blocks.md: ACORN-$\gamma$ pays at build time. **ACORN-1** moves the expansion to search time. Its index is ACORN-$\gamma$'s construction with $\gamma = 1$ and $M_\beta = M$, which the paper describes as the original HNSW index without pruning. At each visited node, the lookup gathers **all one-hop and two-hop neighbors**, applies the predicate, and truncates to $M$.

Intuition: a node with $M$ neighbors has up to about $M^2$ two-hop neighbors, so the expanded neighborhood plays the role of ACORN-$\gamma$'s long list. The cost is that the expanded set is a less precise stand-in for a node's true $M\gamma$ nearest neighbors, and the lookup reads more lists per visited node.

blocks.title: ACORN-1 neighbor lookup at node H

scenes.caption: Lookup at H with M = 2. H's stored list, nearest first, is G, A, I (plain graph from the figure).
First hop u = G. G itself fails the predicate, so it is not added, but its list is still scanned.
G's list: H is skipped (it is v), J passes and is added. This is the two-hop edge that reconnects H to J.
Next u = A, which fails. A's list contains I, which passes, so I is added.
u = I passes but is already in out, and I's list (A, H) adds nothing new. Truncate to M = 2 and return.

blocks.title: ACORN-1: two-hop lookups on the plain graph

scenes.caption: Back to the plain M = 2 graph (an HNSW-like build with no extra edges). ACORN-1 does not change the index; it changes the lookup: one-hop and two-hop neighbors, then filter, then keep M.
At H, neighbor G fails, but G's own list contains J, which passes. The lookup returns J and I. J (4.12) is closer than H (5.83), so move to J.
At J, both neighbors E and G fail. E's list holds D, G's list holds H. The lookup returns D and H. D (3.61) is closer, move to D.
At D, B passes directly (3.16). At B, the lookup finds only D. Search returns B, the true answer, with the same path as ACORN-gamma: I, H, J, D, B.

blocks.md:
**The tradeoff in numbers** (from the paper):

- Search: ACORN-1 reaches about 1.5x to 5x lower QPS than ACORN-$\gamma$ at the same recall. Table 3 counts distance computations to reach Recall@10 = 0.8 on SIFT1M: 611 for ACORN-$\gamma$ vs 999.6 for ACORN-1.
- Build: ACORN-1 builds 9x to 53x faster than ACORN-$\gamma$ (SIFT1M 8.6 s vs 148.9 s; LAION-25M 705.3 s vs 38,007.5 s). In Table 4 it has the lowest build time of all methods, below the HNSW baseline.

The reference code (a fork of FAISS, class `IndexACORNFlat`, whose constructor takes `d, M, gamma`, a per-vector `metadata` list and `M_beta`) implements both variants in the same bottom-level lookup loop: when `gamma == 1` it expands every neighbor, otherwise it expands only entries past `M_beta`. Its README example builds ACORN-$\gamma$ with $\gamma = 12$, $M_\beta = 32$ and ACORN-1 with $\gamma = 1$, $M_\beta = 2M$ (the paper fixes $M_\beta = M$ for ACORN-1).

ACORN-$\gamma$ and ACORN-1 run the same search strategy, predicate subgraph traversal. They differ only in *where* the denser neighborhood comes from: stored at build time (ACORN-$\gamma$, faster search, slower build) or reconstructed from two-hop lookups at query time (ACORN-1, cheap build, somewhat slower search).

blocks.question: A team has an existing HNSW index over 500M vectors and cannot afford a long rebuild. Which approach fits best?
options: ACORN-gamma with gamma = 1/s_min
ACORN-1 style two-hop lookups over a standard HNSW-like graph
StitchedVamana with one graph per label
Raise M in the existing HNSW and rebuild
blocks.explain: ACORN-1 needs no expanded lists at build time; it reconstructs a denser neighborhood during search. Weaviate took this route: its blog says it kept vanilla HNSW indexing so existing data does not need re-indexing. ACORN-gamma and StitchedVamana both require heavier construction, and raising M flattens the hierarchy.

blocks.question: In the codetrace, why is J returned even though J is not in H's stored list?
options: J is H's entry point on the level
J was recovered from H's compressed M_beta entries
Truncation to M adds the next closest node
The lookup reads failing neighbor G's list and J passes the predicate
blocks.explain: ACORN-1 expands every neighbor u of H, including ones that fail, into u's own list, then filters. G fails but links to J, so J appears. There is no M_beta compression in ACORN-1 (it is fixed at M_beta = M).

lessons.title: Choosing gamma, falling back to pre-filter, and real results

blocks.md: **Setting $\gamma$.** The paper's simple rule is $\gamma = 1/s_{\min}$, where $s_{\min}$ is the lowest selectivity the graph should serve. Its experiments match $\gamma$ to each dataset's expected minimum query selectivity: $\gamma = 12$ for SIFT1M and Paper (12 equally likely labels, $s = 0.083$), $\gamma = 30$ for LAION, and $\gamma = 80$ for TripClick. Build time and memory grow with $\gamma$, so you do not want it larger than needed.

**Falling back.** Below $s_{\min}$ the predicate subgraph may disconnect even in ACORN, but those are exactly the queries where pre-filtering is cheap: its cost $sn$ is small. So ACORN uses a cost-based rule: if the estimated selectivity is above $1/\gamma$, search the ACORN index; otherwise pre-filter and brute-force. The paper also suggests a diagnostic: compare hybrid recall with plain HNSW ANN recall at the same $M$ and efc, and if hybrid recall is much worse, increase $\gamma$ from its starting value of $1/s_{\min}$.

scenes.caption: ACORN is configured with a minimum selectivity s_min = 1/gamma. Each query's predicate selectivity is estimated before search.

Example: SIFT1M with gamma = 12, predicate 'label in {1, 2, 3}' passes 3 in 12 records. s = 0.25 is above 1/gamma = 0.083, the expected filtered degree 384 x 0.25 = 96 exceeds M, so the graph is searched.

TripClick's 1st-percentile predicate has s = 0.0127, just above 1/80 = 0.0125 with gamma = 80. Anything below would be pre-filtered: 0.0125 x 1.06M vectors is about 13,200 distances, with perfect recall.
Estimation errors cut both ways: wrongly pre-filtering keeps perfect recall at lower QPS; wrongly searching ACORN gives up the perfect recall pre-filtering would have delivered at similar QPS.

blocks.prompt: Pre-filtering on SIFT1M at s = 1/12 always scans every passing vector. How many distance computations is that, and how does it compare with ACORN-gamma's 611 in Table 3?
blocks.reveal: $sn = 10^6 / 12 \approx 83{,}333$ distance computations, about **136x** ACORN-$\gamma$'s 611 (and it gives perfect recall). Pre-filtering's cost is linear in $sn$, so it only wins when $sn$ is small, which is why the fallback threshold is a selectivity, not a fixed count.

scenes.caption: From the paper's Table 3 (s = 1/12). ACORN-gamma needs 53.5% more than an HNSW built only on the passing points, ACORN-1 151% more, post-filtering 363% more.

blocks.md:
**Reported results** (Recall@10 vs QPS, ACORN, pre- and post-filtering implemented in FAISS-based C++, other baselines from their released code, all on one machine):

- Overall 2x to 1,000x higher QPS at 0.9 recall than prior methods.
- SIFT1M and Paper (12 equality labels): 2x to 10x over Filtered-DiskANN and NHQ.
- TripClick and LAION-1M (date ranges, keyword lists, regex): 30x to 50x over pre- and post-filtering, which the specialized indices cannot run.
- LAION-25M: over three orders of magnitude more QPS than the next baseline.
- Across TripClick selectivity percentiles, 5x to 50x at 0.9 recall, with pre-filtering most competitive at the 1st percentile ($s = 0.0127$).

**How the alternatives differ.** *Filtered-DiskANN* (Gollapudi et al., WWW 2023) builds label-aware Vamana graphs: FilteredVamana prunes with a filter-aware rule and uses a start node per label; StitchedVamana builds one graph per label and overlays them. It handles about 1,000 labels with equality filters. *NHQ* (Wang et al., 2022) builds a composite index and joint pruning over vectors and attributes, and the ACORN paper notes it supports only equality predicates with one attribute per record. ACORN instead never sees predicates at build time, which is why it can serve regex and range filters.

**In production: Weaviate.** Weaviate's engineering blog describes an ACORN filter strategy based on ACORN-1. It keeps vanilla HNSW indexing (so existing data needs no re-index), uses two-hop expansion **only when the connecting node fails the filter**, and randomly seeds extra entry points that match the filter. It is one value of the `filterStrategy` index setting; the docs now list `acorn` as the default, beside the older `sweeping` and a newer `pathseer`. Very restrictive filters still switch to flat brute-force search (the flat-search cutoff). In their tests ACORN helped most when filters and queries had low correlation (up to about 10x), while sweeping won at high correlation and at 50% selectivity.

ACORN is not free accuracy. The paper gives no connectivity guarantee for arbitrary data (neither does HNSW); connectivity is shown empirically. Very selective or strongly clustered predicates still need the pre-filter fallback, and ACORN-$\gamma$'s build is far slower than HNSW (SIFT1M 148.9 s vs 11.3 s, LAION-25M 38,007.5 s vs 1,147.2 s).

blocks.question: Your workload's predicates range from s = 0.002 to 0.6 over 50M vectors. You build ACORN-gamma with M = 32. What is a sensible plan?
options: gamma = 500 so every query uses the graph
gamma = 1/s_min for a moderate s_min such as 0.02 (gamma = 50), and pre-filter anything estimated below 0.02
gamma = 1 and rely on post-filtering for low selectivity
Skip ACORN: pre-filter everything because it is exact
blocks.explain: Pre-filtering at s = 0.02 over 50M is about 1M distances, costly but bounded; going lower makes it cheaper still. gamma = 500 would multiply build time and upper-level memory enormously. Post-filtering is weakest at low selectivity. Pre-filtering everything costs up to 30M distances per query at s = 0.6.

blocks.question: The selectivity estimator says s = 0.05 but the true value is 0.005, below 1/gamma = 0.02. ACORN searches the graph. What is the most likely consequence?
options: Lower recall, because the predicate subgraph may be disconnected where pre-filtering would have been fast and exact
Higher latency but perfect recall
A wrong-type error, since the predicate is not indexed
No effect, because ACORN truncates to M
blocks.explain: At s = 0.005 the expected filtered degree gamma x M x s = 50 x 32 x 0.005 = 8 is far below M, so search may get stuck. The paper notes this direction of error trades away the exactness pre-filtering would have given. The opposite error (pre-filtering when s was high) costs only speed.
